title: Pauri 12, meaning: beyond describing
hookLine: the state of the one who trusts cannot be described; there is no paper or pen for it (Japji 12)

cards: Try explaining why you trust your oldest friend. You start a list. She showed up when my car broke down.
He kept a secret for ten years. Halfway through, you can hear it's not landing. The facts are true, but they're not the thing.

The thing is the ease in your shoulders when that person walks in, and there's no sentence for that. People who try to describe being in love, or holding a newborn, hit the same wall: the words run out.
Pauri 12 says the same happens to the one who trusts, and then it says something bold about writing.

teach.b: Here is Pauri 12, in paraphrase. The state of the one who trusts cannot be told.
Whoever tries to tell it regrets it afterward.

teach.h: NO PAPER, NO PEN, NO WRITER.
teach.b: There's no paper, no pen, no writer who can sit down and capture the state of the one who trusts. Such is the Name of the Stainless One. Only someone who trusts knows it, in their own mind.
Four moves. First, the state can't be told: yesterday's line, mannai kee gat kahee na jaae. Second, the one who tries regrets it.
Not because trying is wrong, but because every description comes out smaller than the thing, and you feel the shrinking as you speak. Third, the surprise: kaagad kalam na likhanhaar.
Paper, pen, writer, all three named and all three set aside. Remember where this is written.

Japji stands at the start of the Guru Granth Sahib, a book Sikhs treat with enormous reverence: carried on the head, wrapped in cloth, read aloud with care. And inside that book, Guru Nanak says writing can't hold this.
Fourth, the refrain that will close each of these four trusting stanzas: such is the Name of the Stainless One, known only to the one who trusts it in the mind.
That's not a secret handshake. It's more like swimming. You can read about water all day.
You only know it from inside.

how: Pauri 12 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning by many Sikhs; its closing lines on the Name of the Stainless One, known only to the one who trusts, return as the refrain of pauris 12 to 15.

s: Pauri 12 says trying to describe trust is forbidden
it says the one who tries regrets it, because every description comes out smaller.
a verse in the Guru Granth Sahib says writing can't hold this state
no paper, no pen, no writer: the scripture points past itself.
the closing lines of Pauri 12 return in pauris 13 to 15
such is the Name of the Stainless One, known to the one who trusts.

games.q: someone hands you paper and a pen and says: write down exactly what it's like to trust. what does Pauri 12 say happens?
o: you write it perfectly if you're a good enough poet.
you try, and you regret it: it can't be told.
you should refuse to talk about it at all.
games.why: whoever tries to tell it regrets it afterward. there's no paper, no pen, no writer for it; it's known only to the one who trusts.

practice: Trust one thing without explaining it: the chair holding you, or the next breath arriving on its own. Let your weight go into the seat, and let the breath come without managing it.
Each time your mind starts to explain why it's safe to trust, drop the explanation and just rest.

wordCard.voice: Gat. The state, the condition: of the one who trusts, it can't be told; no paper, no pen, no writer can hold it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 12: no paper, no pen, no writer.

carryVoice: Your line: no pen for this. Some things stay bigger than the sentence. Day one hundred eighty-three, done.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3 (Japji, Pauri 12, line 3)
